name: Tarrafal camp (Campo do Tarrafal)
subtitle: The Tarrafal camp was built in 1936 at Chão Bom, on Santiago island, as a penal colony for opponents of Portugal's Estado Novo regime.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: On Santiago island, in the village of Chão Bom, municipality of Tarrafal

facts.label: Years of operation
facts.value: Concentration camp in operation between 1936 and 1974 according to this study

facts.label: First phase
facts.value: 1936-38: the first 150 anti-fascist prisoners arrived and lived in canvas tents without minimum hygiene

facts.label: Deaths
facts.value: 34 anti-fascist prisoners died between 1936 and 1954, out of 360 inmates

facts.label: First closure
facts.value: The camp closed on 26 January 1954, but was legally closed only two years later

facts.label: Reopening
facts.value: Reopened in 1961 with the colonial war as a labour camp for African prisoners held for political and ordinary offences

facts.label: After 1974
facts.value: After the Carnation Revolution the PAIGC reopened Tarrafal in December 1974 to imprison its opponents; it closed permanently in July 1975

facts.label: Heritage status
facts.value: National heritage by resolution 33/2006; 29 October designated Anti-fascist Resistance Day

facts.label: UNESCO
facts.value: Museum and national heritage site; on UNESCO's Tentative List since 2004

facts.label: 2021 protocol
facts.value: Portugal and Cape Verde signed a protocol in July 2021 to cooperate on heritage protection, aiming at a World Heritage bid for the former camp

parts.text: The Tarrafal camp was built in 1936 at Chão Bom, on Santiago island, as a penal colony for opponents of Portugal's Estado Novo regime. It operated in phases until 1954, reopened in 1961 for African prisoners during the colonial war, and was briefly used again in 1974-1975. It is now a museum and national heritage site.
